title: Let my people go (Exodus 5:1–9)
hookLine: Moses asks, and Pharaoh makes them gather their own straw
last: I WILL BE WITH YOUR MOUTH.

cards: Four words have traveled a long way from this chapter. Enslaved people in America sang them in a spiritual called Go Down, Moses. Harriet Tubman, who led people out of slavery, was called Moses.
Preachers in the civil rights movement thundered them from pulpits. Let my people go. It sounds like a victory.
But the first time the words are spoken in the Bible, they don't work at all. In fact, they make everything worse.

teach.h: LET THEM HOLD A FEAST TO ME.
teach.b: Moses and Aaron, the reluctant speaker and his brother, walk in to the king of Egypt and say it, in the King James Bible: "Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Let my people go, that they may hold a feast unto me in the wilderness."
Notice the request. Not, set them free forever. Just, let them go and worship.

Pharaoh's answer starts the real contest: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go? I know not the LORD, neither will I let Israel go." Who is the Lord? Pharaoh is about to find out, but not yet.
First he answers a request for relief by adding to the load.

Until now, the slaves were given straw to mix into their bricks. Now: "Ye shall no more give the people straw to make brick, as heretofore: let them go and gather straw for themselves." Same number of bricks.
Find your own straw. They're idle, he says; that's why they cry out about worship. The Israelite foremen are beaten when the bricks fall short.
They turn on Moses and Aaron: you've made us stink in Pharaoh's eyes. And Moses, who didn't want this job, turns to God: why have you done this to your people?
Why did you ever send me? The Bible keeps that complaint. It doesn't hide that doing the right thing can make things worse before they get better.
Christians and Jews have both read this chapter as a picture of how oppression answers a request for freedom.
The people who sang it later knew that. They sang it anyway.

how: In Black churches in America, the Exodus story and the spiritual Go Down, Moses have shaped preaching on freedom and justice, and Christians read the chapter when praying for people who are oppressed.

games.q: you're Pharaoh. two Hebrew brothers ask you to let their people go into the wilderness to worship. what do you do?
o: let them go for three days.
refuse, and make them gather their own straw.
games.why: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?" he takes away their straw and keeps the quota the same.

practice: Think of someone being pushed down right now, a person you know, a group in the news, a worker whose load keeps growing, and picture them gathering straw in the dark.
Then find one true sentence you could say for them, to someone who could help. If you pray, you can pray for them.

wordCard.voice: Pharaoh. The king of Egypt who refused Moses and Aaron's demand to let Israel go, and answered by taking away the straw.

orig.note: Hebrew: send out my people, let my people go.

carryVoice: Your line: who is the Lord? It's Pharaoh's question, and it hangs over every chapter to come. See you tomorrow.
